e.t: Abdedom is a personal name, also rendered “Avthethom.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 12 times across 10 verses, almost entirely in 1 Chronicles, with one occurrence in 2 Chronicles. Its meaning as a name is not further defined by the available lexical information, so the name itself is the supported sense. The precise role of the person in any particular verse requires that verse’s surrounding context.

Abi, also rendered Avi, is a proper name. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, this name occurs once, at 1 Kings 2:46. The available meaning is limited to the name itself, so its significance in that passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage rather than from the name alone.

This noun means “contest” or “contention”: a struggle, dispute, or serious effort in which opposing sides or aims are involved. It can describe conflict between people, but the central idea is an intense contest rather than an ordinary activity. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 17 times, showing a recurring word for struggle or opposition across these books.

Aisan, also rendered Esan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 4:32. Because names primarily identify people, places, or families, its meaning is best understood as the identity of the person it names, not as a general concept to apply elsewhere. The available information does not provide a separate definition beyond the name itself.

This adverb means “faultlessly,” describing an action done without blame or defect. It presents conduct as free from a charge of wrongdoing, rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 3:13. The precise force in that verse depends on its surrounding wording, but its basic sense is clear: something is carried out in a faultless manner.

This Greek LXX verb means to shoot up or grow again. It describes renewed growth, like something sprouting upward after having been cut back, damaged, or previously grown. As a verb, it expresses the act or process of coming up and growing anew rather than merely possessing new life. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Job, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here.

ἄνευ is a preposition meaning “without.” It indicates that someone or something is absent, lacking, or not included in relation to another person, thing, or action. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it appears 42 times, so it is a regularly used way to express the absence of something. Its basic sense remains consistent across its uses, while the surrounding sentence identifies what is absent or lacking.

This verb means “in conflict”: it describes being engaged in opposition or struggle against someone or something. As a verb, it expresses an active state of contending rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 17:14. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense is clear: being in conflict.

This Greek LXX noun means “encounter” or “escort.” It refers either to meeting someone or to accompanying someone, depending on the sentence. The word describes an event or act involving people coming together, whether through a meeting or through an accompanying welcome or departure. It occurs 35 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, showing that it is a recurring term for such meetings or accompanying actions rather than a title, person, or abstract doctrine.

This adjective means “unaffected,” describing someone or something not altered or moved by an outside influence. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Genesis 25:27. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the precise aspect of being unaffected must be understood from that passage’s context. Its basic sense remains clear: it identifies a person or thing that has not been changed, disturbed, or influenced in the relevant situation.

Arari is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. Its meaning is presented simply as “Arari,” so Scripture does not provide a broader ordinary-language definition for it. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs three times, all in 1 Chronicles 11:34, 1 Chronicles 11:35, and 1 Chronicles 11:44. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain each individual reference, but the word itself functions as a personal name.

Arnaphar, also rendered Arnafar, is a proper name referring to an individual rather than a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:36. The available wording preserves the name itself but does not provide a separate definition or description of the person. Its precise significance in that verse therefore depends on the surrounding genealogy and passage context.

Arōniim is a proper name, identifying a named person or place rather than describing an action or quality. Its meaning is given as “Arōniim,” also represented as “Aronim.” In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only once, at Isaiah 15:5. Because no surrounding verse text is available here, the name’s specific referent cannot be identified further from this word alone. Its role is therefore primarily that of a distinguishing name in the passage.

Asarai; Asare is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but as a personal designation. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 23:35. The available lexical information gives the forms “Asarai; Asare,” while the surrounding verse text is not included here, so the person’s specific role or significance cannot be explained from this word alone.

Asennaios, also rendered Asenneos, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or named figure in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Genesis 10:17. The name itself does not provide further meaning or explain the person’s role; those details must come from the surrounding passage and its wider scriptural context.

Asōb, also rendered Asov, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 9:14. Because the passage text is not included here, the name’s particular role in that verse cannot be described further. Its central meaning is therefore its function as a personal name: Asōb or Asov.

gl: function of chief of the court
d: function of chief of the court

e.t: αὐλαρχία refers to the function or office of chief of the court. It is a noun describing an official position connected with serving as the court’s chief, rather than naming the person who holds that position. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at 1 Kings 2:46. Its precise reference there belongs to the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to the chief’s official function or responsibility.

Aunan, also rendered Avnan, is a proper name belonging to a person in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies individuals rather than expressing an action, quality, object, or relationship. The name appears ten times across eight verses, chiefly in Genesis, and also in Numbers and 1 Chronicles. Because it is a personal name, its meaning here is its identifying use: naming Aunan within genealogical and narrative passages. The surrounding verse is needed to distinguish which occurrence and person is intended.

Babylon is the proper name of a city and kingdom known in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general description or action word, but a name identifying a specific place and power. The word occurs 254 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, with especially frequent use in Jeremiah. Its use ranges across historical and prophetic books, so the surrounding verse is needed to understand what is being said about Babylon in any particular passage.

Baux is a proper name, referring to a person named “Baux” (also rendered “Vafks”). It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis 22:21. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader who is being named, not what quality, action, or idea is being expressed. The surrounding verse supplies the person’s specific place in the passage.

This is a proper name, represented as “Bērōthaiou” or “Virotheu.” It identifies a particular person, place, or associated designation rather than describing a general action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within 2 Samuel 4. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the specific referent cannot be identified more precisely from the name alone.

This word is a proper name rendered “Gazaios” or “Gazeos.” It identifies a named person or group in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX, in Joshua 13:3 and Judges 16:2. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific reference in each passage cannot be described further, but its basic function is to designate by name. The two occurrences belong to the Old Testament portion of the LXX corpus.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Gaiphaēl” or “Yefel.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:14. Because the available information does not include the verse text or surrounding context, the name’s particular referent cannot be identified more precisely here. Its normal function is simply to designate that named entity in the passage.

This noun means “jesting,” referring to speech or behavior intended as humor, teasing, or mockery. It names the act or manner of making light remarks rather than describing a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 31:27. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the word itself points to joking or derisive expression.

e.h: A Knower or One Who Knows
e.t: This noun refers to a person who knows—someone possessing knowledge or awareness. It can describe a knower rather than naming the knowledge itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in four separate verses. Its English rendering may appear through a surrounding expression rather than as a direct noun, so the exact way it functions depends on the sentence where it occurs. The central idea remains a person characterized by knowing. Its occurrences are found in 1 Samuel, 2 Kings, and 2 Chronicles.

This Greek LXX verb means “bite”: to use the teeth against something or someone. It describes a concrete physical action rather than an abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material represented here, it occurs 14 times, showing repeated use of this ordinary action word. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the word itself consistently points to biting or being bitten.

διεκβολή is a noun meaning “passing through.” It refers to movement through or across a place, route, or boundary, with attention to the passage itself rather than to a person or object making it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, appearing in Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Obadiah, and Zechariah. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains passage from one side or point through to another.

This noun refers to a feast of rededication or an act of consecration. It describes setting something apart again for a dedicated, sacred purpose. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 12:27, so its exact emphasis there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea is renewal of dedication: something is formally devoted or made holy for its intended service.

This word means “hundred,” referring to a quantity of one hundred. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament when counting people or groups by hundreds. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in passages from 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. Its basic meaning remains numerical: it identifies a group or amount consisting of one hundred, with the surrounding verse supplying the specific people or things being counted.

Elisoub, also rendered Elisuv, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person in the Greek Old Testament text. The name appears six times, in Ezra and Nehemiah, including records connected with priestly or family lines. Because a personal name identifies someone rather than expressing a general idea, its basic meaning here is the person’s name itself: Elisoub or Elisuv.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “fill in” or “fill up.” It describes making something full, supplying what is lacking, or bringing something to fullness. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs 158 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings included in this corpus, so it is a well-attested word with a broad range of uses. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being filled and the surrounding sentence.

This word means “some,” referring to part of a group rather than everyone in it. It is an adjective that identifies an unspecified number or selection of people or things. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 3 Maccabees. The word’s basic sense remains intentionally general: it points to certain members of a larger group without naming exactly which ones or how many. Its precise reference in each passage depends on the surrounding sentence and context.

This verb means “tell out” or “make known,” expressing the act of openly declaring something so it is no longer kept undisclosed. It can describe acknowledging or confessing a matter, as well as announcing information to others. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 12 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its central idea remains consistent while the surrounding passage determines what is being made known.

This verb means to become or be “utterly weak,” describing a condition of complete loss of strength. It points to more than ordinary tiredness: the person or thing is greatly weakened and unable to remain strong. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Psalm 63:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic meaning is complete weakness.

This noun refers to the upper millstone—the stone used at a mill to grind grain. It can also describe something located at the mill. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Deuteronomy and Judges, and both occurrences concern a millstone. The word therefore names a specific working stone rather than a general tool or place. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This adjective means “necessities,” referring to what is needed or required. It functions as a describing word, pointing to necessary things rather than naming an action, person, or place. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs nine times across 1 Chronicles, Wisdom, and the Maccabean books. Its basic sense remains focused on needs or necessary provisions; the surrounding verse determines exactly what necessities are being discussed.

This word is a proper name rendered “Hermōn” or “Ermon,” referring to a named biblical entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 12 times. Its appearances are concentrated in 3 Maccabees, with additional occurrences in Judges, Psalms, and Song of Songs. The exact significance of the name in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to dye something red or make it scarlet. It describes an action involving the application or production of a red color, rather than naming the color as a mere object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 13:14. The basic sense remains focused on coloring something red; the precise role of the verb in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “noble.” It describes someone or something regarded as noble, using a word that expresses elevated worth or standing. Within this LXX corpus, it occurs eight times, appearing in Job and in the books of Maccabees. Its central meaning remains consistent wherever it occurs, while the surrounding sentence determines whether the nobility concerns a person, quality, or circumstance. The English rendering “noble” supports the same basic sense.

gl: good journey; wishes for a good journey
d: good journey; wishes for a good journey

e.t: This Greek LXX noun refers to a good journey or to wishes for someone’s journey to go well. It describes the idea of a favorable, successful passage from one place to another, and it can also express a spoken or wished blessing for that journey. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Proverbs and three times in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Zachōr, also written Zakhor, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 10:13, identifying a person named Zachor. The name itself does not provide a further meaning or describe an action, quality, or event in the information available here. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s place in that record.

e.h: A Word for Or or Than
e.t: This Greek word connects alternatives with the meaning “or,” and it can also compare two things with the meaning “than.” It may function as a conjunction, adverb, or particle, depending on how it relates words or clauses in a sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 4,769 times, showing that it is a common linking word rather than a term naming a person, object, or action. Its exact force is determined by whether the sentence presents a choice or makes a comparison.

This adjective describes someone or something that is partly dead, severely weakened, or close to death. It presents a condition between being alive and fully dead, emphasizing extreme physical decline rather than ordinary tiredness. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 4:11. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly who or what is described there, but the word itself points to a state of near-death and serious weakness.

Iethermath is a proper name, functioning as the personal or identifying name of an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is its name designation rather than a broader concept. Iethermath occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Kings 10:22. The available lexical definition is simply “Iethermath.”

To “approach as a suppliant” means to come before someone humbly as a petitioner, seeking help, mercy, or a favorable hearing. It is a verb describing the act of making such an appeal rather than merely being in need. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs nine times, naming a recurring action of humble pleading. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This proper name identifies the Jordan, appearing in Greek as “Iordanēs” or “Iorthanis.” It functions as a name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 204 times, with especially frequent use in Joshua, Deuteronomy, and Numbers. Its first recorded occurrence is in Genesis 13:10, and its last is in 1 Maccabees 9:48. The exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a personal name: “Iōab” or “Ioav.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 160 times, with most occurrences in 2 Samuel, and it also appears in 1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, 1 Kings, Ezra, and Psalms. Because it is a name, its specific significance in any passage comes from the person being mentioned and the surrounding verse. The word itself primarily functions as that person’s designation.

Iōacha, also rendered Ioakha, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the Greek Septuagint, at 2 Chronicles 29:12. The available information establishes the name’s identity and its single occurrence, but does not provide the surrounding verse text needed to explain that person’s role or significance in the passage.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “clean”: it describes the act of making something clean or removing what makes it unclean. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Samuel, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. The precise force in any one verse depends on what is being cleaned and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means to gather or glean, especially by collecting what remains after a harvest or gathering. It describes the action of picking up or securing what is available rather than leaving it behind. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs eight times, including passages in Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. The wording can therefore describe either gathering generally or gleaning the remaining produce, with the surrounding verse showing which sense is intended.

“Murmur against” means to express dissatisfied or resistant speech directed toward someone or something. It is a verb describing complaint rather than quiet reflection, though the exact force in its single occurrence depends on the surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, this word occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 11:39. Its central idea is opposition voiced through complaining or grumbling, with the complaint aimed against a person, group, or situation.

This verb means “trample”: to tread on something forcefully, often underfoot. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs 47 times across 43 verses, showing that it is used repeatedly for forceful treading. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the act of trampling.

This Greek LXX verb means “decompose” or “corrupt”: to break something down, spoil it, or cause it to become ruined. It can describe damage to a condition, object, or community, depending on the sentence. The word occurs 27 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, beginning in Genesis and continuing through 2 Maccabees. Its central idea is deterioration—something becoming damaged, spoiled, or corrupted rather than remaining sound.

Kilikia is the proper name “Kilikia,” identifying a particular named place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. As a proper noun, it functions like a place-name in a sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, in 1 Maccabees 11:14, 2 Maccabees 4:36, and 4 Maccabees 4:2. The word’s exact significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context.

This Greek LXX verb means “allot”: to give or assign something, often by a deliberate distribution. It describes the act of designating a portion or share rather than merely possessing it. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in two verses: once in 1 Samuel and twice in Isaiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being assigned and to whom, but its central idea remains the giving of a designated portion.

This verb means “tired” or “labor”: it describes becoming weary or working with exertion. It presents effort as something that can leave a person worn down. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Lamentations 5:5. That single occurrence confirms its ordinary sense but does not by itself establish every detail of the verse’s situation; the surrounding passage is needed for that. The word’s basic idea is exertion accompanied by weariness.

Koue, also called Kue, is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint). It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general concept. The name occurs once in the Septuagint, at Ezekiel 23:23. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its specific referent cannot be explained further here; the lexical evidence establishes the name’s identity, not its contextual role.

This verb means “pregnant,” describing a woman who is carrying a child. It expresses the condition of pregnancy rather than a general feeling or action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Ecclesiastes 11:5. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise role in that sentence must be understood from its immediate context, but its central meaning is clear: being pregnant.

Kyros, also rendered Kiros, is a proper name referring to a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 24 times across 20 verses, especially in Ezra, and also in 2 Chronicles, Isaiah, and Daniel. The name is used consistently as an individual designation rather than as a general description, action, or quality. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions simply as a personal name.

This Greek LXX noun means a “covered chariot,” referring to a vehicle enclosed or sheltered by a covering. It is a specific word for a type of chariot rather than a general term for any vehicle. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here: twice in 1 Samuel and once in Isaiah. Because the surrounding verse text is not included, its precise use in each passage cannot be described further, but its basic meaning remains a covered chariot.

Maasia is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, each in a different genealogical or community record. The name is represented in English as “Maasia,” and the available lexical information gives no additional meaning beyond this name designation. Its specific reference is determined by the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

This adverb means “rather” or “more.” It marks a preference, comparison, or stronger degree, showing that one choice or condition is favored over another or exists to a greater extent. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it appears 42 times, so its basic sense is used across a range of statements rather than referring to one special subject. Its precise force in any sentence depends on what is being compared or preferred.【p03:word:lxx:L708448:identity】【p03:word:lxx:L708448:occurrences】

Mari is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is simply the name “Mari.” In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 3:22. Because a personal name identifies someone instead of expressing a general idea, the surrounding verse is needed to identify which person Mari is in that genealogy; the name itself does not carry a broader definition.

This verb means to boast—to speak or act with proud self-importance. It can describe boasting as an action rather than simply naming a boastful person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, three in Psalms and once in Obadiah. Its precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains proud or self-exalting speech. The related noun-like gloss “boaster” points to the person who boasts, while “boast” names the action itself.

This adjective describes something as “within measure”—moderate, limited, or kept within an appropriate boundary. It points to what is neither excessive nor beyond proper proportion. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 31:20. The word’s basic sense is therefore one of restraint and fitting proportion, while the precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and subject.

“Engaged” describes a committed promise to marry. As a verb, it refers to entering or holding that marriage commitment, rather than merely showing personal interest or affection. This word appears eight times in seven verses of the Greek Old Testament, with occurrences in Deuteronomy and Hosea. Its precise emphasis in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains the committed relationship of being engaged.

Mōlid is a personal name, represented in English as “Mōlid” or “Molith.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 2:29. The available information identifies the name and its location, but does not include the surrounding verse text needed to explain anything more about the person or the role the name has in that passage.

Mōrasthi, also written Morasthi, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Micah 1:1. Its spelling identifies the name as it is rendered in this Greek text; the name’s precise referent must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This noun refers to a “treasure?” in the Greek Old Testament. The question mark reflects that the precise meaning is uncertain, but treasure is the recognized basic sense. It occurs only twice in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Kings 20:13 and Isaiah 39:2. Its exact nuance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here. This remains a distinct Greek LXX word and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament term.

This adjective means “withered” or “dry,” describing something from which moisture has departed. It can describe land, ground, or other things in a dried condition. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears 38 times, including descriptions of dry land after waters separate and dry ground through which people pass. Its central idea is not simply age or weakness, but the absence of moisture and the resulting condition of being dry or withered.

This noun refers to kindred or relationship—the bond connecting people as members of the same family or closely related group. It describes a recognized connection between persons, rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 20:19. Its basic sense is therefore a relationship of kinship or belonging, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that relationship is being discussed.

This noun means “common zeal for”—a shared eagerness or ardent concern directed toward the same person, purpose, or matter. It describes zeal held together by more than one person, rather than private enthusiasm standing alone. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 13:25. The exact force of the phrase in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is a united, common zeal focused on something.

This noun refers to an insult or reproach directed against someone. It describes words or treatment that express disgrace, blame, or contempt rather than simple disagreement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 36:3, and is rendered “reproach.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to dishonoring speech or conduct placed upon a person or people.

This Greek LXX adjective means “orphaned,” describing someone who has lost or is without parents. It identifies a person’s vulnerable family condition rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 50 times, especially in passages that recognize the needs of the fatherless and call attention to their treatment. The word can also describe the condition more broadly, so its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording. It belongs to the Greek LXX vocabulary and should not be confused with a Greek New Testament entity.

This adjective describes something filled with broken pieces of pottery, or potsherds. It points to a place or object characterized by many scattered ceramic fragments rather than by smooth, whole material. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Judges 1:35, so its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its direct sense remains concrete: “full of potsherds,” emphasizing an abundance of broken pottery pieces.

Ophimin, also rendered Ofimin, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or group in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs once in the LXX, at Genesis 46:21. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, its specific identity and role in that passage cannot be stated further without adding information beyond the word’s recorded meaning.

This word means “girl” or “maid,” referring to a female servant or young woman. It is a noun used for a person rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears 78 times, showing that it is a recurring term for such a female person. Its exact sense in a particular passage depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains a girl or maid. The word occurs from Genesis through Susanna, including places where “maid” is the English rendering.

“Paradise” refers to a beautiful, life-giving garden or favored place. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is a noun used for such a setting, especially in passages connected with the garden of Eden. The word occurs 33 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, from Genesis through Song of Songs, showing that it can describe both a literal garden and a richly pictured place of beauty. Its exact force in any verse comes from the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “deploy; arrange”: to place people or forces in an ordered position, often so they are prepared for action. It describes deliberate organization rather than random movement. The word occurs 72 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, showing that it is used broadly for arranging or positioning. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being placed and the surrounding context.

This word means hoar-frost or rime—the thin coating of frozen moisture that forms on cold surfaces. It is a noun naming a visible feature of winter weather and can describe frost found on the ground or other objects. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, including passages in Job, Psalms, Daniel, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its basic sense remains a natural phenomenon, while the surrounding verse determines how that frost functions in the sentence.

This adverb means “confidently,” describing an action done with assurance rather than hesitation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Zechariah 14:11. The word tells how an action is carried out, not who performs it or what specific action is being described. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding Greek and English context, which is not included here.

gl: fly over and around; flutter around
d: fly over and around; flutter around

e.t: This Greek verb means “fly over and around” or “flutter around.” It describes movement through the air, emphasizing circling or passing above and around something rather than simply remaining still. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 14:17. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its ordinary sense is aerial movement involving flying or fluttering around.

Persikē, also rendered Persiki, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or named individual in the Greek LXX corpus. This name occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 1:19. Without the verse text and its surrounding context, the name itself does not indicate the person’s role or significance; those details must be understood from the passage where it appears.

This word means “before”. It points to an earlier time or position, showing that one event, action, or condition comes ahead of another. It can function as an adverb or preposition, helping mark sequence or priority in a sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 48 times, including passages from Genesis, Numbers, Samuel, Kings, and Isaiah. Its basic idea remains simple: something happens before something else, whether the focus is time, order, or the point at which another event occurs.

This noun refers to “adoration” or “obeisance”—an expressed act of reverence directed toward someone honored. It describes the posture or practice of bowing before, honoring, or showing deep devotion to a revered person or authority. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs four times, including passages in Ezekiel, Sirach, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and situation.

This verb means to “make as if”—to present oneself as though something were true or to act as though one were in a certain condition. It describes deliberate outward behavior or pretense rather than simply possessing a quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs four times across 1 Samuel, Job, Sirach, and Susanna. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what the person is pretending or acting to be.

This word means a gate—the structure or entrance that provides access through a wall, enclosure, or city. It is a noun used for literal gates in the Greek Old Testament, including gates associated with towns, cities, and other enclosed places. Because it appears 327 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, it represents a broad and recurring biblical term rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains a gate or controlled entrance.

Ramen is a proper name—a place-name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It refers to a specific location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Joshua 15:34. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name itself can be identified, but its particular significance in that passage should be understood from the wider context of Joshua 15.

Roōbōth, also rendered Rhoovoth, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, and its precise referent is determined by the surrounding passage. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. The available lexical wording preserves the name itself, but does not provide an additional definition or explain its etymology.

This proper name refers to a Samaritan woman. It identifies a female person associated with Samaria, rather than describing an action, quality, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, the word occurs three times, all in 1 Maccabees. The gloss identifies the person as “Samareitis” or “Samaritis,” names used for a Samaritan woman. The exact significance of the individual named depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a personal designation connected with Samaria.

Sachania is a proper name, also rendered Sakhania. It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs twice, once in Ezra and once in Nehemiah. Because no surrounding verse text is provided here, the name itself does not supply further information about the person’s character, role, or significance. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name Sachania, with Sakhania as an alternate rendering.

This word is the personal name “Selloum” or “Sellum.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or spiritual idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across four verses, all in 2 Kings 15. The English rendering “Sellum” reflects the same name. Its precise historical role belongs to the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a proper name.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Souman” or “Suman.” It is not a descriptive term or action word, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 4:8. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name itself identifies the person but does not by itself explain that person’s role or significance in the passage.

This adjective means “ashy,” describing something that resembles or has the appearance of ash. It identifies a visible quality rather than an action or a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Genesis, so its known use is limited but consistent. The precise shade or force intended in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains an ash-like appearance.

This verb means “set up as a monument”: to establish something upright as a lasting memorial or marker. It describes an intentional act of setting something in place so it stands as a visible reminder. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, all within seven Old Testament verses, including passages in 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, and Lamentations. The surrounding verse determines what is being established and why, but the word itself emphasizes making something stand as a monument.

This Greek LXX verb means “confine; catch”: it describes shutting something or someone in, restraining movement, or taking hold of them. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, place, or quality. It occurs 41 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing use across many kinds of passages. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on physical confinement, being trapped, or being seized. Its basic idea remains the placing of something within limits or successfully taking hold of it.

This verb means to inform against someone or to extort from them. It describes using accusation or pressure to gain an advantage, rather than dealing honestly. As a verb, it expresses an action directed toward another person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, including passages in Genesis, Leviticus, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, and Ecclesiastes. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central sense remains wrongful accusation or coercive extraction.

This verb means to join in praising—to add one’s voice to praise already being offered. It describes active agreement and participation in honoring or celebrating someone, rather than praise given entirely alone. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it appears two times, both in 3 Maccabees. The word therefore focuses on sharing in praise with others, while the surrounding passage identifies whom the praise is directed toward and why.

This Greek LXX noun means “meeting”—an encounter in which people come together. It names the coming together itself rather than describing a person, place, or action. The word occurs 75 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing that it can describe meetings in many kinds of situations. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on who is coming together and why, but its central sense remains a meeting or encounter.

This adjective means “all together” or “whatsoever,” expressing the whole of something without leaving any part out. It can describe a complete group, collection, or total range of things, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, so its basic sense is consistent but its precise force depends on what it modifies. The word appears most often in 3 Maccabees, and also occurs in Esther and Sirach.

This noun means “putting together” or “arranging.” It describes the act of organizing things, people, or matters into an ordered whole. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it occurs 16 times, so it is used across more than one kind of setting while retaining this central idea of arrangement. Its exact sense in any verse depends on what is being organized and how the surrounding sentence presents it.

This verb describes something as “gangrened”—affected by gangrene, a destructive condition in which tissue decays. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Leviticus 26:16 and Deuteronomy 28:32. Its wording points to a physical condition rather than an attitude, action, or general feeling. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of what is happening.

“Employ art” is the word’s central meaning. As a verb, it describes carrying out an action by using art, rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 46:5. That single occurrence establishes its attested use in this corpus, while the surrounding verse is needed to determine the precise force of the action there. This is a Greek LXX word and should be read within that corpus.

This adjective means “threefold”: involving three parts, three layers, or a set of three. It describes something as having a three-part character rather than merely appearing once or twice. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in four verses, with three occurrences in Ezekiel and one in 2 Kings. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the noun or object it describes, but the central idea remains something arranged or understood in threes.

This verb means “indulge”: to give oneself freely to a desire, pleasure, or activity rather than restrain it. It describes an action or behavior, not a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice, once in Isaiah and once in Sirach. The surrounding verse determines what desire or pleasure is involved in each occurrence.

This adjective means “left behind; staying behind,” describing something or someone that remains after others have gone or been removed. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Isaiah 11:11, so its basic sense is clear but its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word focuses on what remains—the part, people, or thing still present rather than those already gathered or departed. It does not by itself explain why something remains; that detail comes from the context.

This noun means a slayer or murderer: a person who kills another human being. It identifies the person responsible for a killing, whether the surrounding passage uses the broader term “slayer” or the more direct term “murderer.” In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 17 times in 13 verses, especially in Numbers and Deuteronomy, where laws address people involved in killing. The word itself names the killer; the surrounding context determines the circumstances and legal significance of the act.

This adjective means “Chaldaikos,” serving as a descriptive word that identifies something by that designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 1:4. The available meaning identifies the word’s lexical sense, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain precisely what it describes there. Thus, its basic function is descriptive rather than naming an action, quality, or object independently.

Cham, also rendered Kham, is a proper name for a person rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 16 times across 15 verses, with its use concentrated in Genesis and also appearing in 1 Chronicles and Psalms. The name is consistently rendered “Cham” in the available English representation. Its specific significance in any individual passage comes from the surrounding verse and passage, not from a separate descriptive meaning attached to the name itself.

This word means “ravine,” referring to a deep channel or narrow valley, often associated with water flowing through it. As a noun, it identifies the natural feature itself; as an adjective, it describes something connected with such a ravine or watercourse. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 89 times, including references in Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, and 2 Samuel. Its basic meaning remains geographical, while the surrounding verse determines the particular ravine being mentioned.

Chorrath is a proper name, referring to a specific place named in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered “Chorrath” and appears twice, both times in 1 Kings 17—at 1 Kings 17:3 and 1 Kings 17:5. The name itself identifies the place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its lexical function is simply as the name Chorrath.

This noun refers to “unguent” or “anointing”—a substance or practice connected with applying oil. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used especially in passages concerning anointing in Exodus, and it also appears in Daniel and Sirach. Its basic meaning remains focused on the anointing substance or act, while the surrounding verse determines the precise use. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus.

This word means “singer”: a person who sings. It is a noun identifying the person performing the singing, rather than the song itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in 1 Kings, 2 Kings, and 2 Chronicles. Its basic meaning is consistent across these occurrences: it refers to people whose role or activity is singing. The surrounding verse determines the particular occasion, setting, or responsibility connected with that singing.

This adjective means “ripe.” It describes something that has reached the condition of ripeness or readiness, rather than remaining unready or immature. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Job and once in Jeremiah. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its ordinary sense remains focused on being ripe. The word’s identity and meaning are supported by its lexical definition, while its limited occurrence record places it in two Old Testament verses.
